acquisition.why: Cold email to limited companies is legal, and SEO pages or a self-serve per-report site are possible. Higher-value report buyers usually want a call or trust built through outreach first [E].

onboarding.why: A brief form plus client data upload can be templated. Scoping and the UK GDPR terms for uploaded data need a human check.

delivery.why: Agents can run several deep-research tools and cross-check them. Hallucination liability means Ricardo must verify the facts before sending.

billing.why: Stripe payment per report or by subscription is easy to automate.

support.why: Agents can handle revision requests. Disputes about accuracy need a human.

scores.R_why: This suits a technical solo founder and needs little capital; a £300 test is feasible. The weak point is that clients can run ChatGPT, Claude or Perplexity deep research themselves for about £20 a month.
scores.M_why: Generic reports are heavily commoditised by deep-research tools. Headroom exists only in a niche with proprietary data or a UK sector focus [E]. The $1-per-request model risks API costs exceeding the price.
scores.one_line: Highly automatable but commoditised. The only first-hand claims are setup times, with no paying customers or revenue, all from one channel. It is viable only as a narrow UK-niche report product with human fact-checking [E].

acquisition.why: Upwork and Fiverr are legal inbound marketplaces. Proposals, Loom videos and buyer chat effectively need a human, and new accounts get little visibility (the Fiverr test failed). Platform terms also restrict automated bidding and AI delivery [E].

onboarding.why: Each gig requires clarifying the brief with the buyer.

delivery.why: AI drafts most deliverables. Quality control and revisions need a human.

support.why: Back-and-forth with clients and managing reviews is human work.

scores.R_why: 6-8 hours a week is consumed by proposals and client chat. This is labour-for-hire rather than an agent-run business, and pricing is a race to the bottom.
scores.M_why: The market is flooded with 'AI-assisted' sellers and bot-generated proposals. Buyers can increasingly use AI directly.
scores.one_line: Low-cost to try, but it is time-for-money gig work with a failed first-hand Fiverr test and saturated, price-crushed demand. It is a poor fit for an approve-only agent model.

acquisition.why: The app inherits existing App Store search (ASO) traffic, which is inbound and legal. It depends on the Apple/Google algorithm.

onboarding.why: In-app onboarding and paywall need no human.

delivery.why: The software runs itself. Occasional updates and OS compatibility fixes need a developer.

support.why: Agents can triage reviews and email. Refunds go through Apple.

scores.R_why: At 2-4x annual earnings, any app with meaningful revenue costs thousands, far beyond the £300 test budget. Due diligence also needs skill and time [E].
scores.M_why: Underpriced indie apps on brokers still exist. Competition from app-flipping buyers is rising, and Apple's paywall rules add risk.
scores.one_line: The automation profile of an owned app is excellent, but buying one is out of budget. The 5x revenue jump is a single guest's success story from one video [E].

acquisition.why: Deal sites and the App Store are inbound but platform-dependent. Rank-spiking tactics draw Apple scrutiny.

onboarding.why: This is in-app and software-led if run on your own app.

delivery.why: It is a tactic applied to an app. Sold as a service to app owners, it becomes consulting [E].

billing.why: Web checkout via Stripe or app store billing is automated.

support.why: Support is mostly the app's own support.

scores.R_why: This is a growth tactic rather than a standalone business and needs an existing app first. Web-to-app checkout rules are still in flux in the UK and EU.
scores.M_why: Lifetime-deal rank boosts are a known trick, and Apple flags abnormal activity. Web checkout is becoming mainstream, so the edge is shrinking.
scores.one_line: A tactic, not a business. The single client success story ($200 to $7k a month) is uncorroborated, and Apple flagged the activity. It is useful only if Ricardo already owns an app.

acquisition.why: Organic social content is legal inbound, and agents can generate and schedule posts. It is fully dependent on platform algorithms and AI-content policies.

delivery.why: Generation can be automated. Concepts, trend picking and reference videos need human input, and quality varies.

billing.why: Platform payouts are automatic but tiny. Brand deals require human negotiation and ASA #ad compliance.

support.why: Comment moderation is light and can be automated.

scores.R_why: Cheap and agent-friendly, but RPMs of $0.05-0.30 mean huge view counts are needed. UK eligibility for creator payout programmes varies, and AI disclosure rules are tightening.
scores.M_why: The barrier to entry is near zero and the space is flooded. Platforms are demonetising unoriginal or inauthentic AI content.
scores.one_line: Easily automated but lottery-like economics. The '$50-500 per reel' claim needs roughly 170k-5M views per reel [E]. The content is partly tool-promotional (the Higgsfield Earn programme), and platform risk is high.

acquisition.why: App stores and paid social are legal inbound channels, though paid installs are expensive. Text check-ins require opt-in consent.

delivery.why: The LLM chatbot runs unattended. Wellbeing safety guardrails need monitoring.

billing.why: App store or Stripe subscriptions handle billing.

support.why: Agents can handle FAQs. Sensitive wellbeing conversations need escalation.

scores.R_why: Ricardo can build it. The £300 budget won't buy meaningful paid acquisition, and privacy and health-claim boundaries apply in the UK.
scores.M_why: Fitness and habit AI coaches are saturated, and ChatGPT, Gemini and fitness apps with built-in AI substitute directly.
scores.one_line: A brainstormed idea with no customers or revenue, from one channel and one extractor. Automation is good, but the space is crowded and general AI assistants already replace it.

acquisition.why: Referrals and ads that lead to sales calls are human-led. Cold email to limited companies is legal, but many UK local businesses are sole traders (PECR applies).

onboarding.why: Kickoff calls, site access and strategy need a human.

delivery.why: Agents can write content and do keyword work. Strategy, backlink vetting and quality control remain human.

support.why: Monthly reporting can be automated, but client calls and churn management cannot.

scores.R_why: Ricardo has the skills, but retainer clients expect communication and results that 6-8 hours a week struggles to support. Results take months to show.
scores.M_why: The market is crowded, and AI search and AI Overviews are eroding SEO value. Mass AI content risks Google penalties.
scores.one_line: Corroborated real revenues across 9 first-hand videos, but it is a client-service business with a heavy human load. SEO is declining in the AI-search era, so it fits the approve-only model poorly.

acquisition.why: Upwork and LinkedIn inbound profiles and cold email to limited companies are legal. Winning bespoke projects needs calls and referrals.

onboarding.why: Process discovery and system access are per client.

delivery.why: Claude Code and n8n agents can build much of the work. Testing in the client's systems and scoping are human.

billing.why: Invoicing per project or retainer is easy to automate.

support.why: Broken workflows and scope creep require human fixes.

scores.R_why: This fits Ricardo's technical skills and needs nearly zero capital. Hours are the constraint, so it works only with productised small builds such as form-to-CRM [E].
scores.M_why: UK small businesses have real demand and project prices ($1-20k claimed) are healthy. Competition is growing, and clients are increasingly able to build with AI themselves.
scores.one_line: The best skill fit here, with credible first-hand pricing. It is still bespoke service work; a productised, fixed-scope offer to UK limited companies could make it semi-agent-run [E].
